title: Storing and Serving
description: Keeping a bottle well, serving it at the right temperature and saving what's left.
L: What wine needs while it waits
Name the four conditions for good storage
Explain why bottles are stored on their side
Decide which wines are worth keeping

Wine keeps best somewhere cool, ideally 10 to 15 degrees Celsius, dark, free of vibration and with a steady temperature. A cupboard away from the oven is better than the top of the fridge or a sunny shelf. Strong light, especially sunlight, can damage wine in days.

Heat speeds up the chemistry of ageing, so a wine kept at 25 degrees ages several times faster and can taste cooked. Swings in temperature make the wine expand and contract, pushing air past the cork. Light, especially ultraviolet, breaks down compounds in the wine and causes a fault called light strike, which smells of cabbage.
Heat and light age wine too fast
Which of these are good conditions for storing wine?
Cool, steady, dark and still. Sun and the oven bring heat and light, the two main enemies.

Bottles with natural cork are stored on their side so the wine keeps the cork moist; a dry cork shrinks and lets air in. Screw caps can stand up. And most wine is made to drink within a year or two. Only a small share, such as good Bordeaux or vintage Port, improves for decades.
Cork on its side; screw cap any way
Most wines improve if you keep them for ten years.
Not true. Most wine is made to be drunk young, within a year or two. Only wines with enough concentration, acidity or tannin improve over many years.
Store wine cool, dark, still and at a steady temperature
Heat, light and temperature swings damage wine
Lay corked bottles on their side, and drink most wines young
Why a few degrees change a wine
Name the right temperature for each style
Chill or warm a wine quickly

Sparkling wines are best well chilled, 6 to 10 degrees Celsius. Light whites and rosés, 7 to 10. Fuller whites, 10 to 13. Light reds, 13 to 15. Medium and full reds, 15 to 18. Room temperature in a modern heated home, often 21 or more, is too warm for most reds.

Cold hides aromas and makes tannin and bitterness feel harsher, but it lifts freshness and keeps bubbles fine. Warmth releases aromas and softens tannin, but too much makes alcohol taste hot and flabby. That's why light whites go cold and tannic reds go warmer.
Why is a tannic red usually served warmer than a white?
Cold emphasises tannin and bitterness. A few degrees warmer and the red feels smoother and more aromatic.
Fifteen minutes in the fridge brings a red from a warm room down to cellar temperature. To chill a white fast, put it in a bucket of ice and water, not ice alone; water touches the whole bottle.
Match each wine to its serving temperature.
Bubbles coldest, full reds warmest, everything else in between.
Serve sparkling coldest and full reds warmest
Cold sharpens tannin and hides aroma; warmth releases aroma
Ice plus water chills fast; a short spell in the fridge helps reds
Choose a glass that helps a wine show well
Open still and sparkling wines safely

A good glass has a bowl that narrows at the top, to gather aromas, and a stem so your hand doesn't warm the wine. Fill to about a third so you can swirl. Larger bowls suit aromatic reds; narrower ones keep whites cool. A tall flute keeps bubbles but hides aroma, so many prefer a white wine glass for Champagne.
Bowl that narrows, a stem, a third full

A bottle of Champagne holds about 6 atmospheres of pressure. If the cork is released fast, it can leave at over 40 km/h. Keep a thumb on the cork, point it away from people, and twist the bottle, not the cork, letting the gas out with a sigh rather than a pop.
Twist the bottle, not the cork
Put the steps for opening a sparkling wine in order.
Loosen the wire cage, thumb on the cork
Tilt the bottle away from people
Let the cork ease out with a sigh
Keeping the thumb on the cork from the moment the cage loosens is the key safety step.

Pouring a wine into a decanter does two jobs. It separates an old red or vintage Port from its sediment, the solids that form with age. And it gives a young, tight wine air, which can open up its aromas. Pour slowly in front of a light and stop when you see sediment reach the neck.
Decant for sediment or for air
Decanting is only useful for very old wines.
Not true. Old wines are decanted for sediment, but young, tannic reds are often decanted for air, which helps their aromas open.
A bowl that narrows, a stem and a third full help any wine
Open sparkling wine by holding the cork and twisting the bottle
Decant old wines for sediment and young ones for air
Explain what happens to an open bottle
Know how long each style lasts once open

Once opened, wine meets oxygen. At first that can help, but over days it flattens fruit and turns the wine dull, nutty or vinegary. Bacteria can turn alcohol into acetic acid, the acid of vinegar. Cold slows all of this, so the fridge is the best place for any open bottle, red included.

Light whites and rosés usually stay pleasant for 2 to 3 days in the fridge with the cork back in. Reds, 3 to 5 days, because tannin protects them. Sparkling wine keeps its fizz for 1 to 3 days with a proper stopper. Fortified wines last longest: an opened tawny Port or Madeira can keep for weeks, Madeira for months.
Which opened wine is likely to keep longest?
Madeira has already been exposed to heat and oxygen in its making, and its high acidity and alcohol protect it. It can last months once opened.
Pour leftovers into a smaller bottle so there's less air above the wine. Less air, slower decline. The spoon in the neck of a sparkling bottle is a myth; a hinged stopper works.
Leftover red wine keeps longer if stored in the ____.
Cold slows oxidation and bacteria. Take a red out half an hour before serving.
Oxygen slowly flattens an open wine
Keep open bottles closed and in the fridge, reds included
Fortified wines last longest; light whites and sparkling the least
Serve each style at the right temperature
Open, decant and keep wine properly
Which conditions damage a stored wine?
Light, heat and swings age or damage wine. Darkness is what it needs.
Match each wine to its best temperature.
Why are corked bottles stored on their side?
A moist cork stays tight. A dry one shrinks and lets air in.
Young, tannic reds can benefit from decanting.
Yes. Air helps a tight young red open up. Old wines are decanted mainly for sediment.
Order these opened wines from shortest to longest life in the fridge.
Bubbles fade first, then light whites. Tannin helps reds, and Madeira's making leaves it almost immune to air.
Store wine cool, dark, still and steady
Serve sparkling coldest and full reds warmest
Decant for sediment or for air
Recork and refrigerate leftovers; fortified wines last longest
